word:lxx:L700161.explanation: This word means “holiness”: the quality or condition of being holy. It is a noun used to name holiness itself, and its rendering remains consistent across all five occurrences in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here. The word appears four times in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees, showing its use in language that speaks about what is holy. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700266.explanation: Adida is a proper name, also identified with the form Athitha. It functions as a name rather than as a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees. The available references preserve the rendering Adida, while the lexical identification also records Athitha. The name appears in 1 Maccabees 12:38 and 13:13, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific person or place being named.

word:lxx:L700363.explanation: This adjective describes something that is “unfounded” or “unlawful”—without a valid basis or contrary to what is permitted. It can characterize an action, claim, or condition as lacking rightful support or violating an established rule. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something unjustified or forbidden.

word:lxx:L700437.explanation: This word means “cat,” referring to the familiar domestic animal. It is a noun, so it names the animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:21. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the particular significance of that occurrence must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L700495.explanation: Aitōb, also rendered Etov, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 11:11. The name identifies a person in that passage, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the details needed to understand that person’s role. Its meaning is therefore its identification as a proper name, not a general concept or instruction.

word:lxx:L700572.explanation: This noun refers to a “darter” or “javelin-man”—someone whose role is to throw a javelin in battle. It identifies a person by military function rather than describing an emotion, action, or general weapon. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, at 1 Samuel 31:3. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its precise role in that passage, but the word itself points to a soldier skilled in using or throwing a javelin.

word:lxx:L700598.explanation: This adverb means “accurately,” describing an action done correctly, precisely, or in agreement with the facts. It tells the reader how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Deuteronomy and once in Wisdom. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains careful correctness and precision.

word:lxx:L700806.explanation: This word means “carelessly,” describing an action done without sufficient attention, care, or concern. As an adverb, it explains how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is acting in a careless or heedless manner.

word:lxx:L700891.explanation: This adjective means “ambidextrous”: able to use either hand with comparable skill. It describes a person whose ability is not limited to one preferred hand. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Judges. The basic idea is a two-sided or both-handed ability, while the surrounding verse determines what person or action the adjective describes.

word:lxx:L700943.explanation: This verb means to “seek again”: to look for someone or something once more. It describes renewed searching rather than a first attempt to find something. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Job and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being sought and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a repeated or renewed search. [p03:word:lxx:L700943:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700943:occurrences]

word:lxx:L701052.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “draw up”: to pull or lift something upward. It describes upward movement rather than simply remaining in place, and its exact application depends on what is being drawn up in the sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in Daniel, Amos, and Habakkuk. Its basic sense remains focused on bringing something from a lower position upward.

word:lxx:L701139.explanation: This adjective describes something that is out of reach or unattainable. It refers to what cannot be reached, obtained, or accomplished within the situation being described. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), in 3 Maccabees 2:15. Its basic sense remains focused on impossibility of attainment rather than on a particular emotion, event, or spiritual condition. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being called unattainable there.

word:lxx:L701247.explanation: This noun means “relief”: help or support that eases distress, pressure, or need. It names the assistance a person receives when facing difficulty rather than describing the difficulty itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, including passages in Psalms, 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and Sirach. Its precise shade depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the receiving or provision of needed relief.

word:lxx:L701290.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “unbearable,” describing something that cannot reasonably be endured or carried. It presents a situation, burden, or demand as too difficult to withstand. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Exodus 18:18, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: the matter in view is beyond what a person can continue bearing.

word:lxx:L701504.explanation: This LXX Greek verb means “take away” or “receive.” It describes an action in which something is taken, removed, or accepted, depending on the sentence. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including Numbers, Isaiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on what is being taken or received in that context.

word:lxx:L701548.explanation: This noun means “wandering; error,” describing a departure from the right path or a mistaken course. It can refer either to roaming away or to being wrong in one’s direction or judgment. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is movement or direction that has gone astray.

word:lxx:L701625.explanation: This verb means to “avert evil by sacrifice.” It describes an action intended to turn away or prevent evil through a sacrificial act. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 16:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on seeking protection from evil by means of sacrifice. It is an action word, focusing on what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or condition.

word:lxx:L701650.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that remains steady and does not falter. It conveys dependable firmness rather than hesitation, failure, or wavering. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees, so its central sense is clear even though the individual passages are not provided. The word functions as a description, marking a person or thing as consistently reliable and steadfast. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L701669.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “head” or “chief,” referring to one who stands foremost or leads others. Its basic sense can describe a person recognized as having prominence or authority. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 24:31. Since the word appears only there, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L701687.explanation: Araourites is a name rendered Saraurite.

word:lxx:L701733.explanation: Arēsa, also written “Arisa,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament record. This name occurs twice in the Septuagint, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Because the available information gives the name but no surrounding verse text, it does not establish the person’s role, family, or significance. Those details must be understood from the passages where the name appears.

word:lxx:L701867.explanation: This word means “spice,” referring to an aromatic substance used for fragrance, flavor, or ceremonial purposes. It is a noun naming such materials rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, including passages involving stored spices, gifts, burial preparations, and fragrant imagery. Its precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an aromatic spice or mixture of spices.

word:lxx:L701889.explanation: Asaremoth is a noun preserved as a name-like term, with the gloss “Hasaremot?” indicating uncertainty about its precise identification. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Jeremiah 38:40. Since the available wording does not provide a broader definition or surrounding verse text, its ordinary meaning cannot be expanded beyond this proper-name rendering. The term is therefore best understood as an uncertain name or designation rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or general object.

word:lxx:L701993.explanation: Asrōni, also rendered Azroni, is a proper name used to identify a person or family group in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice, both times in Numbers 26, so its role is as a specific designation rather than a general description or action. The name is preserved as a name in English rather than translated into an ordinary meaning-word. Its precise reference in each occurrence depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L702057.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to an occupation or business—the work or activity with which a person is engaged. Its sense is practical and broad, naming what someone is occupied with rather than identifying a particular profession. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines the precise aspect of that occupation or business being discussed.

word:lxx:L702080.explanation: This adjective means “childless,” describing a person or household without children. It refers specifically to the absence of offspring, rather than serving as a general word for loneliness, barrenness, or lack of descendants unless the surrounding passage gives that sense. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs six times, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the same: having no children.

word:lxx:L702138.explanation: This verb means to spend the night, describing remaining somewhere through the nighttime rather than leaving immediately. It can refer simply to lodging or staying overnight, and its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 41 times, showing that this is a recurring word for overnight stay. The word is also used in passages translated from both historical and poetic portions of the Greek Old Testament.

word:lxx:L702174.explanation: Aphairema refers to a separate offering.

word:lxx:L702251.explanation: This adjective describes something or someone as “without grace.” It expresses the absence of grace or graciousness, rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 20:19. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic meaning remains a lack of grace. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

word:lxx:L702303.explanation: Achlia, also written Akhlia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:41. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a broader definition or explain the individual’s role. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L702435.explanation: Baithsour, also rendered Vethsur, is a proper name for a place or locality in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary descriptive word or an action; it identifies a named location. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The precise significance of the place in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its broader setting.

word:lxx:L702440.explanation: This word is a proper name rather than a general description. It is given in the forms “Baithchor” and “Vethkhor,” which identify the same named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 7:11. Without the verse text, its specific reference cannot be described further here, but its basic function is to name rather than express an action, quality, or general idea.

word:lxx:L702497.explanation: This noun refers to dye—the substance or liquid in which something is dipped. It names the material used to color an object by immersing it, rather than the object being colored or the act of dipping itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Judges 5:30. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is the dye or coloring substance associated with dipping.

word:lxx:L702707.explanation: This word is a proper name for a place called “Bērōtha” or “Virotha.” It is not presented as a common description or action, but as the name of a specific location in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Ezekiel 47:16, and its precise significance there depends on the surrounding passage and the geographical setting described by Ezekiel. The name itself identifies the place rather than expressing a general quality, event, or spiritual concept.

word:lxx:L702862.explanation: Gabee is the name of a place.

word:lxx:L702888.explanation: This noun refers to soothsayers—people regarded as able to reveal hidden knowledge or predict events through divination. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Daniel, where it is used as a recognized category of specialists consulted for mysterious matters. The word identifies a type of person rather than describing a specific prediction or method. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L702916.explanation: Gaisos means a spear or javelin.

word:lxx:L702981.explanation: This Greek LXX noun describes arrogance or exultation—a proud sense of superiority or joyful triumph. Its meaning can point either to boastful self-importance or to an elevated, celebrating spirit, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Job and twice in Sirach. Because the individual verse texts are not provided here, the precise emphasis in each occurrence cannot be stated, but the central idea remains a heightened attitude expressed through pride or exultation.

word:lxx:L703010.explanation: Geththaios, also rendered Yeththeos, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 12 times in 12 verses, from Joshua through 1 Chronicles. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular reference must be determined from each passage. The name occurs especially in 2 Samuel, where it appears seven times.

word:lxx:L703029.explanation: This adjective describes something ridiculous or absurd—something that appears plainly foolish, unreasonable, or worthy of scorn. It is a descriptive word, used to characterize a person’s words, reasoning, or action rather than name a separate object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what the surrounding sentence identifies as foolish or unreasonable.

word:lxx:L703344.explanation: This verb means “tithe”: to give a tenth as an offering. It describes the act of setting apart and presenting one-tenth of something, especially in worship or support of God’s appointed service. As a verb, it expresses what a person does rather than naming the offering itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:38, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the available verse text does not provide further context.

word:lxx:L703414.explanation: This noun refers to one of the people—a commoner rather than someone identified by rank or special status. It describes a person as belonging to the ordinary population. In the Greek of the Septuagint’s deuterocanonical books, it occurs once, at Wisdom 18:11. That single occurrence confirms its basic social meaning, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular force there. Its central idea is an ordinary member of the people.

word:lxx:L703577.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to “equipment” or “furniture”—the movable items prepared for use in a place or activity. It can describe physical furnishings or necessary gear, depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including Exodus 31:7 and 2 Maccabees 11:10. Its precise application in either verse depends on the verse’s immediate context, but its central idea remains the set of things arranged or provided for practical use.

word:lxx:L703599.explanation: Diasōzō means to save thoroughly or bring safely through.

word:lxx:L703656.explanation: Diegeirō means to arouse or rouse.

word:lxx:L703784.explanation: This noun means “deceit” or “subtlety”: misleading behavior that hides the truth or uses crafty means to mislead someone. It describes dishonesty as a quality or practice rather than a single spoken falsehood. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Numbers, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains cunning deception.

word:lxx:L703915.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “lifting up” or “pride.” It refers to being raised up, or to an elevated attitude that exalts itself. Its basic idea can describe elevation in a straightforward sense or an inward posture of self-importance, depending on the sentence. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 19:25. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which aspect is intended there.

word:lxx:L703959.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “consecration” or “dedication”: the setting apart of something for a sacred purpose. It names the act or occasion of dedicating something to God, rather than describing a person, object, or feeling by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 7:88. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the formal dedication of something for holy use.

word:lxx:L703960.explanation: This verb means “burn”: it describes setting something alight or causing it to be consumed by fire. It presents burning as an action rather than naming the fire or the object involved. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:29. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being burned and how the action functions in that passage.

word:lxx:L704293.explanation: Ekporeuomai means to emerge or travel out.

word:lxx:L704367.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “cry out”: to call aloud or express words in a strong, audible outcry. It describes an action of speaking publicly or forcefully, rather than simply mentioning something quietly. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all within Daniel 2, so its established sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in each occurrence depends on the immediate sentence and passage context.

word:lxx:L704389.explanation: This noun refers to a silver fir, a kind of fir tree. It names a physical tree rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs eight times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Psalms, Ezekiel, and other books. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the silver fir itself.

word:lxx:L704411.explanation: Eleasa is a proper name rendered “Eleasa.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in Old Testament verses. The available references are in 1 Chronicles and Jeremiah, but verse text is not included, so those references do not establish additional meaning beyond its role as a proper name.

word:lxx:L704486.explanation: Elisaph is a personal name, also rendered Elisaf. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears seven times, chiefly in Numbers and once in Ezra. The available wording establishes the person’s name, but not its deeper name meaning or the individual details of each occurrence. Its precise significance in any passage must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

word:lxx:L704653.explanation: ἔναντι means in someone's presence or before them.

word:lxx:L704705.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “see in”: it describes seeing or looking within something. As a verb, it expresses an act of perception rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, at Genesis 20:10. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an act of seeing inward or within.

word:lxx:L704749.explanation: Enistēmi means to be present or to be set in.

word:lxx:L704846.explanation: This verb means “sharpen”: to make something keen or pointed, especially an edge or weapon. It describes an action rather than a person, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 21:16. The central idea is purposeful preparation by making something sharper and more effective. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, whose text is not included here.

word:lxx:L704990.explanation: Heortē means a festival or feast.

word:lxx:L705135.explanation: This verb means “strive for” or “search for”—to actively seek something, pursue it, or look for it. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, it can describe purposeful seeking rather than a merely casual glance. Its 16 occurrences span the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so the basic idea is broad enough to cover both searching for a person or thing and earnestly pursuing a desired outcome. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is most natural.

word:lxx:L705140.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “consider,” describing the act of giving something thoughtful attention. It points to deliberate reflection rather than a passing glance or immediate reaction. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 1:30. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise emphasis in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic sense remains thoughtful consideration.

word:lxx:L705179.explanation: “Adjudicate” means to make a formal judgment or decision, especially when a matter must be settled. It is a verb describing the act of deciding an issue rather than the person or authority who decides it. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, in two different verses. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here; the word itself points to judgment that settles a matter.

word:lxx:L705207.explanation: This noun means “staying on” or “tarrying”—remaining in a place or continuing rather than departing. It describes continued presence or delay, and its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding context. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 38:27. The word therefore points to the act or condition of remaining, lingering, or continuing in place, rather than to a person, object, or separate action. Its meaning is concise: persistence in staying or a period of waiting.

word:lxx:L705438.explanation: “Ermōniim; Ermonim” is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a particular place or geographic feature in the Greek Old Testament wording. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Psalms 41:7. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise identification and significance in that passage cannot be explained further from the word alone.

word:lxx:L705557.explanation: This word means “well” or “rightly,” expressing approval or affirming that something is done correctly. It can function as an adverb, describing the manner of an action, or as an interjection expressing a response such as approval. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across nine verses, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a positive acknowledgment that something is good, proper, or rightly done.

word:lxx:L705580.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to “Euzai,” also given as “Efze.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a named person or designation in the Greek LXX wording. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Nehemiah 3:25. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be stated from the word alone.

word:lxx:L705751.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something with a white speck on it. It refers to a visible white marking or spot, rather than expressing an action or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 21:20. Because it is an adjective, its role is to describe a person or thing by this outward feature. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its list of described conditions.

word:lxx:L705971.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to age or adulthood—the stage or measure of a person’s life. It can describe how old someone is or the maturity associated with adult life. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with “age” appearing as a translation in several passages. Its broad use includes references from Job, Ezekiel, and the Maccabean books, while the exact sense in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L706071.explanation: Thale is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:25. Because the available lexical meaning is simply the name itself and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its personal identity and role must be understood from that passage’s context. The name is therefore best read as a recorded personal designation, not as a word with a broader ordinary definition.

word:lxx:L706220.explanation: Thersa is a personal name. It is also a place name.

word:lxx:L706255.explanation: This adverb means “fiercely.” It describes an action done with intense, wild, or forceful energy, rather than calmly or gently. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:15. The word itself tells how an action is carried out; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the action and explain its particular force there. It is therefore a manner word, modifying the event or behavior being described.

word:lxx:L706394.explanation: Iakaba, also rendered Iakava, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Septuagint text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:36. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is its identifying function: it distinguishes the individual named in that genealogy or list. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role there.

word:lxx:L706462.explanation: This word is the personal name “Iapheth,” also rendered “Iafeth.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, appearing nine times in Genesis and twice in 1 Chronicles. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 5:32, and its last is 1 Chronicles 1:5. The name itself does not describe a quality or concept; it identifies a particular person in the biblical genealogical record.

word:lxx:L706488.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Idiēl; Ithil.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:2. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its personal identity and role must be understood from that passage rather than from the name alone.

word:lxx:L706516.explanation: “Iebosthe” or “Ievosthe” is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs five times in the Greek text, all in 2 Samuel. The available references show its use in 2 Samuel 2 and 23, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s role or situation in each passage.

word:lxx:L706581.explanation: Ieldaph, also rendered Ielthaf, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Kings 23:36. Because the supplied information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role must be determined from that passage. The name itself carries no additional lexical definition beyond identifying the named individual.

word:lxx:L706673.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered as “Iessiou” or “Iessiu.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Samuel 14:49 and once in 2 Chronicles 26:22. The name’s precise identity and role depend on the surrounding passage, since the word itself functions simply as a personal designation.

word:lxx:L706718.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun means “one who comes to seek protection; suppliant”—a person who approaches another for refuge, help, or favor. It describes someone appealing for protection rather than acting as a self-sufficient authority. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including Psalms, Malachi, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on whom the suppliant approaches and what protection or appeal the surrounding text describes.

word:lxx:L706835.explanation: Isoui, also identified as Isoi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It refers to an individual in the Old Testament Greek (LXX) tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:30. Its basic function is to distinguish one person from others in the genealogy or list where it appears.

word:lxx:L706840.explanation: “Israelite” refers to a person belonging to Israel or identifies something associated with an Israelite. It can function as a noun for the person or as a description of identity. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, this word occurs 12 times, appearing mainly in the Old Testament portion and once in 4 Maccabees. Its occurrences include passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, and Psalms. The basic meaning remains a plain identifier of Israelite identity rather than a separate title or action.

word:lxx:L706897.explanation: Ioasar is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 2:18. The available lexical information preserves the name as “Iōasar” or “Ioasar,” but does not provide a further definition or explain the name’s meaning. word:lxx:L706912.explanation: Iōzabad, also rendered Iozavath, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its exact significance for any one occurrence must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

word:lxx:L707076.explanation: This word refers to a gecko, also described as a spotted lizard. It is a noun naming a small crawling creature rather than an action or quality. Those references show that the word belongs to ordinary animal vocabulary, while the exact significance of either passage depends on the verse and its surrounding text. Its central meaning remains the creature itself: a gecko or spotted lizard.

word:lxx:L707142.explanation: This verb means to “hearten” someone or to “ravish the heart of someone.” It describes an action that strongly affects another person’s inner feelings, either by strengthening the heart or deeply captivating it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Song of Songs 4:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a powerful effect on another person’s heart.

word:lxx:L707227.explanation: This verb means “break,” describing the act of causing something to split, crack, or be broken. It presents breaking as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel and Zechariah. The exact object being broken and the force or purpose of the action must be understood from the surrounding verse, since the word itself gives the basic action but not every detail of the situation.

word:lxx:L707285.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “cut down/up”: it describes cutting something down or bringing it down. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. The precise object being cut or brought down depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains forceful downward cutting or destruction.

word:lxx:L707515.explanation: Katergazomai means to accomplish or cultivate.

word:lxx:L707559.explanation: Katōthen means from below, or up from below.

word:lxx:L707623.explanation: This Greek verb means “mix”: to combine substances or ingredients so they become a blended preparation. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on what is being combined, but the central idea remains bringing separate things together.

word:lxx:L707726.explanation: This noun means “heir”: a person entitled to receive what is passed down from another. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from Judges, 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, Micah, and Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L707814.explanation: Koniorton is a name for dust.

word:lxx:L707977.explanation: This adjective means “dog-like,” describing something associated with or resembling a dog. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 25:3. Its meaning is therefore best kept to the stated sense: dog-like, functioning as an adjective that describes a person or thing.

word:lxx:L707999.explanation: This word describes something curved or arched rather than straight. Its basic meaning remains physical and descriptive; the surrounding verse determines exactly what curved or arched object is being mentioned.

word:lxx:L708033.explanation: This Greek Old Testament adjective means “mute” or “dull.” It can describe someone unable to speak, and it can also describe a lack of responsiveness or sharpness. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Psalms, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force depends on what it describes in a sentence: a person, a bodily ability, or a condition marked by dullness. The basic idea remains an absence of normal speech or perceptive responsiveness.

word:lxx:L708125.explanation: Leemi is a proper name rendered as “Leemi.” As a name, it identifies rather than describes an action, quality, or object in the ordinary way a common noun does. This Greek LXX word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 20:5. Its specific role in that verse is understood from the passage itself, but the word’s basic lexical function is simply to designate the name Leemi.

word:lxx:L708150.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “have leprosy,” describing a person affected by that disease. It functions as an action or condition word rather than a name or title. The word therefore identifies the presence of leprosy, while the surrounding passage determines what is happening to the person and why the condition matters there.

word:lxx:L708187.explanation: This verb means “mix with frankincense.” It describes adding or combining something with frankincense, the fragrant substance used in biblical worship and offerings. word:lxx:L708204.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “winnow” or “drive away.” It describes an action of separating or removing, with the specific emphasis determined by the surrounding sentence. Its basic sense remains focused on moving something away or separating it, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in Amos 9:9 must be understood from that passage’s immediate context.

word:lxx:L708248.explanation: Loipos means the rest or what remains.

word:lxx:L708341.explanation: This word means a “cook-shop,” a place where food is prepared or sold. Without the surrounding verse text, the word’s basic meaning is clear, while the exact details of how the cook-shop functions in those verses must come from the passage’s wider context.

word:lxx:L708446.explanation: This Greek LXX adverb means “especially,” marking one person, thing, or point as more notable or important than others in the sentence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what it is emphasizing, but its central idea remains focused distinction: something is especially prominent, preferred, or noteworthy.

word:lxx:L708590.explanation: Machabēna, also rendered Makhavina, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L708600.explanation: Maches is a proper name, rendered “Maches” or “Makhes.” It functions as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its exact referent is therefore best understood from the surrounding passage rather than by assigning it an additional definition.

word:lxx:L708639.explanation: This adjective describes someone who boasts or talks big—using proud, exaggerated, or self-important speech. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning is clear: boastful speech or a boastful speaker.

word:lxx:L708675.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “drunken,” describing someone affected by excessive alcohol or showing the condition of intoxication. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action or object. The word occurs five times in the LXX corpus, in Proverbs, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the condition of being drunken.

word:lxx:L708752.explanation: Meros means a part of something.

word:lxx:L708811.explanation: This adverb means “between” or “meantime,” indicating an interval, position, or situation separating two things or moments. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something situated between or happening in the meantime.

word:lxx:L709001.explanation: Monon means only. It can also mean alone.

word:lxx:L709096.explanation: Mola is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:33. The precise referent of the name belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, while the word itself functions as a preserved name in the Greek text.

word:lxx:L709108.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Mōrēd” or “Morith.” It is not a common noun describing an object, action, or quality, so its meaning is primarily the identification of that individual. word:lxx:L709144.explanation: Nabouzardan is a personal name. The person bearing this name is identified as the captain of the guard.

word:lxx:L709210.explanation: Naphag, also rendered Nafag, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L709265.explanation: This word refers to a falcon, a bird of prey. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, where its precise role depends on the surrounding passage. Because the available lexical definition is specific, its central meaning is simply the bird itself rather than an abstract quality, action, or title.

word:lxx:L709456.explanation: This verb means “make,” describing the act of producing, preparing, or arranging something. It is a practical action word rather than a title or description of a person. Its use includes language about making or preparing, while the exact object and force depend on the sentence where it appears. word:lxx:L709522.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as deeply deserving pity, sorrow, or lament. word:lxx:L709584.explanation: Ollymi means to destroy or make an end of something.

word:lxx:L709777.explanation: Orpha, also written Orfa, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. word:lxx:L709799.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “scent” or “odour”—a smell that can be perceived. It names the fragrance or odor itself rather than an action. word:lxx:L709823.explanation: This word is a proper name referring to Ouel, also given as Oil. word:lxx:L710043.explanation: This verb means to entrust someone to another person or to commit someone into another’s care. word:lxx:L710278.explanation: This noun refers to something made ripe or ready by the sun—literally, something “cooked by the sun; ripe.” It describes fruit or produce that has reached maturity through exposure to the sun, rather than something still unready. word:lxx:L710292.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “plate with silver,” describing the act of covering or furnishing an object with a silver surface. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the object being described, but its central idea remains applying silver as an outer covering or finish.

word:lxx:L710317.explanation: This verb means to wrap something around oneself or to gird up, especially by securing clothing around the body. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being wrapped or what activity the person is preparing to undertake.

word:lxx:L710483.explanation: Pisteuō means to believe. It can also mean to entrust or place trust in someone or something.

word:lxx:L710502.explanation: This noun refers to something formed or devised—a contrivance or a form. word:lxx:L710609.explanation: This noun refers to besieging: placing a city or fortified place under siege. word:lxx:L710630.explanation: Polylogia means wordiness, or the use of many words.

word:lxx:L710713.explanation: This word means “bailiff,” referring to an officer who carries out an authority’s orders or manages an assigned duty. word:lxx:L710861.explanation: This verb expresses the act of “despatch besides”—sending someone or something additionally, alongside what has already been sent or arranged. word:lxx:L710928.explanation: The word means “confirm possession”: it describes the act of establishing or affirming that something is possessed or belongs to someone. word:lxx:L710964.explanation: This noun refers to one who stands before others—a front-rank man or person who takes a leading position. The surrounding passage determines whether the word points to a particular leader or a person holding a prominent place.

word:lxx:L711127.explanation: Raassōn is a proper name, referring to a person named Raassōn, also rendered Rhaasson. It is not a general term describing an object, action, or quality. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to identify the person bearing this name.

word:lxx:L711185.explanation: This verb means “stitch together”: it describes joining separate pieces by stitching them into one. word:lxx:L711242.explanation: Rhegma means ruin, especially something torn apart into pieces.

word:lxx:L711376.explanation: Sadōm is a name, appearing as Sadon in a list of cities.

word:lxx:L711615.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered as “Seddada” or “Seththatha.” It identifies a named place or person rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. word:lxx:L711659.explanation: Selmōn, also rendered Selmon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. word:lxx:L711721.explanation: Sephela is a proper name, also rendered Sefila, rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L711822.explanation: This Greek verb means to “stir up” or “hoe,” describing the action of agitating or working the soil. word:lxx:L711884.explanation: This verb means “become dark” or “remain in darkness.” It describes darkness coming upon something or someone, or a state in which light is absent. word:lxx:L711956.explanation: Souia, also rendered Soia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity cannot be clarified further, but its basic function is simply to serve as a personal designation.

word:lxx:L712056.explanation: This LXX Greek verb means “cover”: to place something over another thing or to provide covering. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being covered and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L712184.explanation: This noun means “relatives,” referring to people connected by family ties or shared ancestry. It describes kin as a group rather than one individual family member. word:lxx:L712214.explanation: This verb means “strike with,” describing an action performed by using something as the means of striking. word:lxx:L712258.explanation: This noun means false accusation or oppression: wrongdoing that unjustly charges, pressures, or crushes another person. word:lxx:L712377.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “sing with”: it describes joining another person or group in singing rather than singing alone. word:lxx:L712399.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “head off with” or “lead off with,” describing the act of departing while taking someone or something along. word:lxx:L712401.explanation: This verb means to hide something together with something else. It describes concealed items sharing the same hiding place or being hidden alongside another thing. word:lxx:L712629.explanation: Sōthala, also written Sothala, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L712827.explanation: This word means “ashes,” the powdery remains left after something has been burned. It is a noun naming that material rather than an action or quality. word:lxx:L712885.explanation: Tolman is a proper name, identifying a person or named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L713103.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something “commanding under”—exercising command while remaining under a higher authority. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the person or thing being described.

word:lxx:L713257.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something shuddering slightly or being seized by a light shudder. word:lxx:L713280.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun refers to something made by weaving, especially a woven robe or a web. word:lxx:L713338.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to someone identified as “Phaltia” or “Faltia.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. word:lxx:L713507.explanation: This noun means “love-charm”: something associated with love or used as a charm in connection with it.
